proposals.subject: Bathynomus giganteus
proposals.title: A smaller present
proposals.content: Swam back with a fish head for her. Had to hold it right against my mouth. I have brought her a smaller fish head and an explanation.
proposals.review: The exact image carries the bodily contradiction: swimming requires holding the food beside the mouth. The intended gift, nibbling and partner are fiction. This is appetite undermining generosity, not another heavy landing or shared-meal complaint.

media.sourceCaption:
This giant isopod (Bathynomous giganteus) was seen snacking on a fish head during Dive 11 of the 2019 Southeastern U.S. Deep-sea Exploration. These deep-sea scavengers are close relatives of the pill bugs, rolly pollies, and sowbugs found in houses and gardens, but Bathynomus giganteus is much, much larger, growing up to a foot and a half in length. Although giant isopods have been known to exist for more than a century, we still don’t know all that much about their biology or behavior, making capturing videos like this one incredibly important (and also really cool).
Learn more
media.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2019 Southeastern U.S. Deep-sea Exploration

proposals.subject: Graneledone boreopacifica
proposals.title: Still interesting
proposals.content: Lifted off to get away from the staring thing. It rose with me. I have never worked this hard to remain exactly as interesting.
proposals.review: NOAA records a swimming getaway from the ROV. The fictional frustration develops her encounter with attention through a new locomotor scene. Swimming must precede brooding. Editorial risk: hold if observer-annoyance feels too close to her earlier light episode.

media.sourceCaption:
At a depth of 2,395 meters (1.5 miles), we had our second Graneledone boreopacifica octopus sighting of the 2023 Shakedown + EXPRESS West Coast Exploration expedition, also during Dive 04. Unlike the earlier encounter, where the octopus was observed ambling across the seafloor, this octopus swam up into the water column, making a quick getaway from the remotely operated vehicle.
Learn more

proposals.subject: Graneledone boreopacifica
proposals.title: Small movements
proposals.content: Something moved inside an egg. I reached for it, stopped, and put my arm against the rock instead. It moved again. I have been trying very hard to give them a quiet mother.
proposals.review: Visible eggs, curled maternal arms and the matching dive caption support brooding. NOAA says baby eyes and arms could be seen within eggs. The response is fiction. Put this last in Gilda chronology; later roaming would contradict her commitment. Payoff is her familiar urge to investigate becoming deliberate restraint for someone else.

media.sourceCaption: A mother octopus seen is guarding a clutch of eggs attached to a rock in Noyes Canyon during Dive 12 of the Alaska Seascape 5 Expedition. Two octopods were seen guarding clutches of eggs on this rock. The octopus seen in this picture looked healthier with more pigmentation, so it is thought that she has been guarding eggs for less time. Upon close inspection, the eyes and tentacles of the baby octopods can be seen within the eggs.

proposals.subject: Limulus polyphemus
proposals.title: Both ways
proposals.content: Followed the wave inland until it left without me. When it came back I turned around to follow it out. It is taking this opportunity to come inland again.
proposals.review: Exact shallow wash supports the setting, but the wave-reversal joke is slight and lacks the weight of the stronger barnacle or rescue scenes. Do not count as a strong proposal simply because image and anatomy fit.

proposals.subject: Limulus polyphemus
proposals.title: Unwilling passengers
proposals.content: The water thinned over my back and all the little mouths shut. I had been trying to get away from the waves. Now I am following one out with everybody closed.
proposals.review: The barnacle-covered body in thin water supports the reversal from resisting waves to seeking water for attached lives. Fiction supplies awareness and intention, not a claim that the source documents barnacle rescue. Do not describe an auditory quiet or assert that he sees his own dorsal surface.

proposals.subject: Limulus polyphemus
proposals.title: The hand stayed
proposals.content: Every time I pulled a leg free, another one tightened. Then the enormous hand stopped me moving. I fought that too, until it lifted one thin loop and two of my legs could disagree again.
proposals.review: Strong exact line-removal contact and restrained recovery scene. However, NPS API Public domain / Full conflicts with credit Used with permission. Hold until rights are resolved by authoritative clarification. No successful release is claimed; the pictured moment is still being untangled.

proposals.subject: Chaceon sp.
proposals.title: Under the other claw
proposals.content: Raised a claw at the thing crawling under my mouth. It ducked beneath my other claw. I am beginning to understand how large I am from its point of view, and it is not helping.
proposals.review: Visible small amphipods around the mouth and underside plus open claw anchor scale and ineffective threat. Specific movement is fiction. Do not call them parasites or cleaners, despite casual infestation wording in the source.

proposals.subject: Chaceon sp.
proposals.title: All at once
proposals.content: Picked up one egg and brought the whole soft cluster to my mouth. The little things on my face came forward. I had been hoping to eat this without anybody standing on the food.
proposals.review: The image is excellent and literal fit is strong, but the payoff returns to tiny companions sharing a meal, a mechanism explicitly excluded from this batch. Keep the image as unused evidence rather than counting the draft.

media.sourceCaption: During a Windows to the Deep 2019 dive to explore a small canyon off the coast of North Carolina at 920 meters (3,018 feet) depth, we came upon a Chaceon crab perched above a white patch on the seafloor. A closer look revealed the patch to be a cluster of hundreds of eggs, proposed to have been deposited on the rock by a pallid sculpin. As we watched, the crab plucked eggs from the pile with its major chelipeds (clawed legs) and ate them. Furthermore, we observed dozens of amphipods (distant crustacean relatives of the crab) clinging to and crawling over the crab’s mouthparts. For the full story, check out this mission log.
media.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Windows to the Deep 2019

proposals.subject: Chaceon sp.
proposals.title: Still touching
proposals.content: Asked the crab behind me to stop touching my back. He shifted. Something touched my back again. There is an anemone here with considerably more hands than he has.
proposals.review: Several crabs and overhanging anemone tentacles support a mistaken source of contact. Movement and complaint are fictional. No sting, friendship or mating is asserted. This is an error of attribution, not shelter fit or a communal meal.

proposals.subject: Muusoctopus sp.
proposals.title: The arms underneath
proposals.content: Raised four arms to make myself enormous. The others kept hold of the mud. I would like whoever is coming to believe I can afford to let go.
proposals.review: The raised web and remaining substrate contact are the exact visible conflict. NOAA scientists did not determine posture function; this is imagined fear, not a biological claim that the photograph depicts defense. Editorial risk: quiet rather than comic, and must earn itself through the divided bodily response.

Learn more

proposals.subject: Muusoctopus sp.
proposals.title: A little less octopus
proposals.content: The brittle stars scattered when I came round the stone. I stopped, pulled my arms closer, and waited. One came back. I am trying very hard not to reach for it.
proposals.review: The exact video poster shows curled arms, a small rock and surrounding brittle stars; source records their movement. Returning visitor and restraint are fiction. Hold: the relational restraint repeats Gilda 03 too closely. Keep the exact image as a lead for a different event; do not admit both drafts.

media.sourceCaption:
At a depth of 1,650 meters (5,414 feet), during the seventh dive of the 2023 Shakedown + EXPRESS West Coast Exploration expedition, we came upon this deep-sea octopus in the genus Muusoctopus. It didn’t seem too bothered or impressed by the presence of remotely operated vehicle Deep Discoverer, but if you look closely at the seafloor around it, you’ll notice several brittle stars who had other ideas and are on the move!
Learn more
media.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2023 Shakedown + EXPRESS West Coast Exploration

proposals.subject: Homolidae carrier crab
proposals.title: A better view of me
proposals.content: They kept looking, so I lifted the coral higher. Now they could see my face. Lowered it again. I can no longer see whether it worked.
proposals.review: The raised fragment, rear-leg grip and eyes beneath it make this an actual concealment problem. The behavior purpose remains fictional because NOAA calls defense a hypothesis. New profile has only this incident, so lead may hold the identity despite the good photo.

media.sourceCaption: Carrier crabs like this one seen during the first dive of the second Voyage to the Ridge 2022 expedition at a depth of 574 meters (1,883 feet), belong to the family Homolidae. They have a specially modified fifth pair of legs that allow them to carry objects on their backs. This particular crab was carrying a piece of coral. It is thought that this behavior may be a defense mechanism, to ward off predators.
media.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Voyage to the Ridge 2022

sourceReview.sourceCaption: This giant isopod (Bathynomus giganteus) was spotted during a Gulf of Mexico 2017 expedition dive to explore an area informally named “Okeanos Ridge,” as it was first mapped using NOAA Ship Okeanos Explorer in 2012. Related to the terrestrial pill bugs often found scurrying around any backyard, species in the genus Bathynomus are the largest of any isopod. The giant isopod in this image was nearly 30 centimeters (11.8 inches) in length!
sourceReview.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Gulf of Mexico 2017
sourceReview.visibleScene: A close giant isopod fills the frame beside dark coral branches and rock.
sourceReview.review: Attractive armor and coral, but no sufficiently distinct event beyond a possible invented brushing encounter.

sourceReview.sourceCaption:

These deep-sea scavengers are close relatives of the pill bugs, rolly pollies, and sowbugs found in houses and gardens, but Bathynomus giganteus is much, much larger, growing up to a foot and a half in length. Although giant isopods have been known to exist for more than a century, we still don’t know all that much about their biology or behavior, making any observations of them incredibly important (and also really cool).
sourceReview.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2019 Southeastern U.S. Deep-sea Exploration

sourceReview.sourceCaption:
Sofia Ledin (NIOZ) and Jennie McClain-Counts (USGS) examine the bait fish after the short-term deployment. sourceReview.sourceCaption: We observed this commensal relationship between a hermit crab and anemone during Dive 11 of the Papahānaumokuākea ROV and Mapping expedition at a depth of 529 meters (1,735 feet). The shell-bearing anemone, Stylobates aeneus, which builds a proteinaceous, gold-colored shell that grows along with the crab, negating the need to change shells over time.

sourceReview.sourceCaption: Mmmm! We observed this crab snacking on a shrimp during Dive 07 of the Seascape Alaska 3 expedition at a depth of 768 meters (2,120 feet). Everyone has to eat, and in the deep ocean where food is often scarce, nothing goes to waste!

sourceReview.sourceCaption: This golden crab was seen during a Windows to the Deep 2018 dive to investigate knoll/mounding features that are fairly characteristic of this region of the Blake Plateau. sourceReview.sourceCaption:
This otherworldly swimming sea cucumber (Enypniastes eximia) was seen at a depth of 1,203 meters (3,947 feet) during a dive off the west coast of Oahu during the Beyond the Blue: 2025 ROV and Mapping Shakedown. While it has no official common name, this sea cucumber, whose scientific name translates to “remarkable dreamer” is often referred to as the “headless chicken monster” due to its unique appearance.
Visit How to Make Any Picture Your Computer or Phone’s Wallpaper for instructions on how to make this wallpaper yours.
Other wallpaper images are available in the Multimedia Library (Media Type: Wallpaper).
sourceReview.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2025 Beyond the Blue
sourceReview.visibleScene: A translucent swimming sea cucumber shows its gut against dark water; a conspicuous NOAA logo occupies a corner.
sourceReview.review: Logo and no new incident; do not use translucent anatomy alone as a story.

sourceReview.sourceCaption:
The swimming sea cucumber, Enypniastes eximia, sometimes referred to as the “headless chicken monster,” is a widespread species present in the abyss. It is encountered widely around the world with records from the Gulf of Mexico, Tropical Atlantic, East Atlantic, New Zealand, and the Southern Ocean (Antarctica). This one was seen off Puerto Rico in 2018.
Swimming sea cucumbers have a special ‘flap’ which they use to ‘lift’ themselves off the seafloor. The transparent body reveals the sediment-filled intestine looping around from the mouth (top) to the anus (bottom).
From: Holothurian Hill.
sourceReview.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Exploring Deep-sea Habitats off Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands
sourceReview.visibleScene: A reddish Enypniastes swims above the bottom in blue water.
sourceReview.review: Already cataloged in nell-vera-twelve media; exact SHA1 match.

sourceReview.visibleScene: A red Chaceon crab raises an open claw; numerous tiny pale amphipods cling to the underside of its legs and mouthparts.
sourceReview.review: Visible small amphipods around the mouth and underside plus open claw anchor scale and ineffective threat. Specific movement is fiction. Do not call them parasites or cleaners, despite casual infestation wording in the source.

sourceReview.sourceCaption: This hungry red crab (Chaceon quinquedens) was lucky enough to nab the head of an Illex squid for a meal. It quickly scurried away from remotely operated vehicle Deep Discoverer at 977 meters (3,205 feet) during Dive 09 of Windows to the Deep 2021.
sourceReview.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Windows to the Deep 2021
sourceReview.visibleScene: A distant red crab carries squid remains; oversized scientific text covers much of the small video poster.
sourceReview.review: Large scientific overlay and tiny crab; reject for feed.

sourceReview.sourceCaption: During a Windows to the Deep 2019 dive to explore a small canyon off the coast of North Carolina at 920 meters (3,018 feet) depth, we came upon a Chaceon crab perched above a white patch on the seafloor. A closer look revealed the patch to be a cluster of hundreds of eggs, proposed to have been deposited on the rock by a pallid sculpin. As we watched, the crab plucked eggs from the pile with its major chelipeds (clawed legs) and ate them. Furthermore, we observed dozens of amphipods (distant crustacean relatives of the crab) clinging to and crawling over the crab’s mouthparts. For the full story, check out this mission log.
sourceReview.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Windows to the Deep 2019
sourceReview.visibleScene: A red Chaceon crab holds a cluster of round white fish eggs at its mouth with a claw. Small amphipods are visible nearby.
sourceReview.review: The image is excellent and literal fit is strong, but the payoff returns to tiny companions sharing a meal, a mechanism explicitly excluded from this batch. Keep the image as unused evidence rather than counting the draft.

sourceReview.sourceCaption:
Towards the end of Dive 11 of the 2021 North Atlantic Stepping Stones expedition, we moved from stable ripples and pavement to softer sediments with smaller fractions of broken paleo reef. The seafloor here was pockmarked with circular patches of turned-over sediments, and we also observed larger scar marks that were likely feeding holds for fish and/or Chaceon crabs — like the one pictured here.
Learn more
sourceReview.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2021 North Atlantic Stepping Stones
sourceReview.visibleScene: A Chaceon crab holds its claws outward on sediment, alone.
sourceReview.review: Portrait posture only.

sourceReview.sourceCaption:
Sea anemones and crabs (Chaceon sp.) seen while diving in Hudson Canyon during the 2021 ROV Shakedown.


Learn more
sourceReview.attribution: Image courtesy of NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2021 ROV Shakedown.
sourceReview.visibleScene: Four red Chaceon crabs occupy a small rock among large pink anemones. Anemone tentacles hang immediately behind the crabs.
sourceReview.review: Several crabs and overhanging anemone tentacles support a mistaken source of contact. Movement and complaint are fictional. No sting, friendship or mating is asserted. This is an error of attribution, not shelter fit or a communal meal.

sourceReview.sourceTitle: Genus Eguchipsammia Living On Top of Dead Coral Rubble
sourceReview.sourceCaption: The view throughout much of the first dive of the second Voyage to the Ridge 2022 expedition was brightly colored yellow coral in the genus Eguchipsammia living on top of dead coral rubble, with sponges, black corals, and carrier crabs sprinkled throughout.
sourceReview.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Voyage to the Ridge 2022
sourceReview.visibleScene: A wide yellow Eguchipsammia coral field covers pale dead rubble; no individual carrier crab is clearly resolved.
sourceReview.review: No resolved crab; attractive habitat cannot stand in for carrying.

sourceReview.sourceCaption:
This octopod (Muusoctopus sp.) was observed at 2,800 meters (9,185 feet) during Dive 05 of the Seascape Alaska 3 expedition stretching out its arms. There was some discussion amongst participating scientists as to what this behavior could indicate and whether it might be predatory or defensive.
Learn more
sourceReview.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Seascape Alaska
sourceReview.visibleScene: A pale Muusoctopus lifts several arms and stretches its web upward while other arms remain on the mud. NOAA did not establish the posture function.
sourceReview.review: The raised web and remaining substrate contact are the exact visible conflict. NOAA scientists did not determine posture function; this is imagined fear, not a biological claim that the photograph depicts defense. Editorial risk: quiet rather than comic, and must earn itself through the divided bodily response.

sourceReview.sourceCaption: A mother octopus seen is guarding a clutch of eggs attached to a rock in Noyes Canyon during Dive 12 of the Alaska Seascape 5 Expedition. Two octopods were seen guarding clutches of eggs on this rock. The octopus seen in this picture looked healthier with more pigmentation, so it is thought that she has been guarding eggs for less time. Upon close inspection, the eyes and tentacles of the baby octopods can be seen within the eggs.
sourceReview.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Seascape Alaska
sourceReview.visibleScene: A purple warty octopus broods large pale eggs attached to a rock face. Single rows of suckers show on curled arms; an anemone sits below.
sourceReview.review: Visible eggs, curled maternal arms and the matching dive caption support brooding. NOAA says baby eyes and arms could be seen within eggs. The response is fiction. Put this last in Gilda chronology; later roaming would contradict her commitment. Payoff is her familiar urge to investigate becoming deliberate restraint for someone else.

sourceReview.sourceCaption:
At a depth of 1,650 meters (5,414 feet), during the seventh dive of the 2023 Shakedown + EXPRESS West Coast Exploration expedition, we came upon this deep-sea octopus in the genus Muusoctopus. It didn’t seem too bothered or impressed by the presence of remotely operated vehicle Deep Discoverer, but if you look closely at the seafloor around it, you’ll notice several brittle stars who had other ideas and are on the move!
Learn more
sourceReview.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2023 Shakedown + EXPRESS West Coast Exploration
sourceReview.visibleScene: A pale Muusoctopus curls its arms near a small rock on mud, surrounded by scattered brittle stars. The published video caption records the brittle stars moving.
sourceReview.review: The exact video poster shows curled arms, a small rock and surrounding brittle stars; source records their movement. Returning visitor and restraint are fiction. Hold: the relational restraint repeats Gilda 03 too closely. Keep the exact image as a lead for a different event; do not admit both drafts.

sourceReview.sourceCaption:
At a depth of 2,395 meters (1.5 miles), we had our second Graneledone boreopacifica octopus sighting of the 2023 Shakedown + EXPRESS West Coast Exploration expedition, also during Dive 04. Unlike the earlier encounter, where the octopus was observed ambling across the seafloor, this octopus swam up into the water column, making a quick getaway from the remotely operated vehicle.
Learn more
sourceReview.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2023 Shakedown + EXPRESS West Coast Exploration
sourceReview.visibleScene: A Graneledone swims above the sediment with web spread and arms trailing in different directions.
sourceReview.review: NOAA records a swimming getaway from the ROV. The fictional frustration develops her encounter with attention through a new locomotor scene. Swimming must precede brooding. Editorial risk: hold if observer-annoyance feels too close to her earlier light episode.

sourceReview.sourceCaption: A stare down with this octopus (Mussoctopus sp.), occurred during Dive 08 of the Seascape Alaska 5 expedition. As we observed it, the octopus displayed its abilities to change color using specialized cells in its skin called chromatophores. It flashed the deep reddish purple seen here before turning completely white within seconds.
sourceReview.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Seascape Alaska
sourceReview.visibleScene: An extreme purple Muusoctopus face close-up shows two eyes, skin texture and curled suckers at the foreground edge.
sourceReview.review: Useful color-change observation, but prose has no new event; extreme close-up avatar crop also failed at 48 px.

sourceReview.sourceCaption:
Observed at a depth of 1,598 meters (5,243 feet), the arms of this octopus in the genus Muusoctopus framed it perfectly for the shot. Seen on the side of a canyon wall during the seventh dive of the 2023 Shakedown + EXPRESS West Coast Exploration expedition.
Learn more
sourceReview.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 2023 Shakedown + EXPRESS West Coast Exploratio
sourceReview.visibleScene: A compact pale Muusoctopus clings to a canyon wall with curled arms around its mantle; a small orange anemone sits beside it.
sourceReview.review: Avatar only, not a standalone episode: compact whole octopus works in the circle, but resting pose does not establish a new event.

sourceReview.sourceCaption:
Three individuals of a large group of sea urchins seen during Dive 08 of the third Voyage to the Ridge 2022 expedition. Note the debris “hats” directly on top of the body. Scientists commented that since each individual had debris in exactly this place, it was too consistent to be incidental.
Learn more
sourceReview.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Voyage to the Ridge 2022
sourceReview.visibleScene: Three dome-shaped Conolampas urchins wear little piles of debris on top.
sourceReview.review: Debris hats are real but no earned narrative event or compatible established species; no fifth identity.

sourceReview.sourceCaption:
An image of a rarely observed gathering of the deep-sea urchin Conolampas sigsbei, as seen during Dive 08 of the third Voyage to the Ridge 2022 expedition. The black-and-white photo was edited with increased contrast to highlight the trails the sea urchins have made in the soft sediment.
Learn more
sourceReview.attribution: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Voyage to the Ridge 2022
sourceReview.visibleScene: A side-by-side color and contrast-enhanced monochrome scientific comparison shows small urchins and sediment trails.
sourceReview.review: Scientific comparison panel, not a gorgeous standalone photograph.

sourceReview.sourceCaption:
Fishing line visible across stony coral and a pencil urchin. Observed during an Illuminating Biodiversity in Deep Waters of Puerto Rico 2022 expedition dive.
Learn more
sourceReview.attribution: Illuminating Biodiversity in Deep Waters of Puerto Rico 2022
sourceReview.visibleScene: Fishing lines span rocky coral habitat; a pencil urchin is small near the top of the frame.
sourceReview.review: Urchin too small and coral context too broad; no valid existing-body mapping.
